questions.q: In adult Basic Life Support (BLS), what is the recommended chest compression-to-ventilation ratio for a single rescuer before an advanced airway is placed?
options: Continuous compressions at 100/min with no breaths in every single-rescuer adult arrest
questions.explain: Adult BLS guidelines specify 30 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths (30:2) at a rate of 100-120 compressions per minute and a depth of 5-6 cm.

open.q: State the recommended compression-to-ventilation ratio for adult Basic Life Support prior to advanced airway placement.

questions.q: Which pair of cardiac arrest rhythms is classified as shockable and requires immediate unsynchronized direct-current defibrillation?
options: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
Sinus bradycardia and complete heart block
questions.explain: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia are disorganized or rapid ventricular rhythms amenable to defibrillation, whereas asystole and PEA are non-shockable rhythms managed with high-quality CPR and adrenaline.

open.q: Name the two shockable cardiac arrest rhythms in the Advanced Life Support algorithm.
accept: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia

questions.q: What is the standard intravenous dose and dosing interval of adrenaline (epinephrine) during adult Advanced Life Support cardiac arrest resuscitation?
options: 1 mg IV (10 mL of 1:10,000) every 3 to 5 minutes
questions.explain: Adrenaline 1 mg IV (10 mL of 1:10,000 solution) is given every 3-5 minutes (alternate 2-minute CPR cycles) to increase coronary and cerebral perfusion pressure via alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction.

open.q: State the standard adult intravenous dose and frequency of adrenaline during cardiac arrest resuscitation.

questions.q: Which antiarrhythmic drug and initial intravenous bolus dose is administered after the third unsuccessful shock in refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia?
questions.explain: Amiodarone 300 mg IV is given after 3 defibrillation shocks for shock-refractory VF/pVT, with a further 150 mg IV dose if VF/pVT persists after 5 shocks.

open.q: Which antiarrhythmic drug and initial dose is indicated after the third shock in refractory ventricular fibrillation?

questions.q: During resuscitation of a patient with pulseless electrical activity (PEA), clinicians systematically screen for the '4 Hs and 4 Ts'. Which condition is one of the '4 Ts' of reversible cardiac arrest causes?
questions.explain: The 4 Hs are Hypoxia, Hypovolaemia, Hypo-/hyperkalaemia (and metabolic disorders), and Hypothermia; the 4 Ts are Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, and Thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary).

open.q: List the four 'T' reversible causes of cardiac arrest screened during Advanced Life Support.
accept: Tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, toxins, coronary or pulmonary thrombosis

questions.q: What is the immediate first-line pharmacological treatment and route of administration for acute severe anaphylaxis in an adult?
options: IV hydrocortisone as sole initial treatment
IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral thigh
Nebulised salbutamol as the only treatment
questions.explain: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1,000) into the mid-anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis) rapidly reverses bronchospasm, laryngeal oedema, and vasodilatory shock; antihistamines and steroids are secondary adjuncts.

open.q: State the first-line drug, adult dose, concentration, and route of administration for acute anaphylaxis.

questions.q: Which airway opening manoeuvre is indicated in an unconscious trauma patient with suspected cervical spine injury?
options: Jaw thrust with manual in-line cervical stabilisation
questions.explain: The jaw-thrust lifts the mandible forward to relieve tongue-induced airway obstruction without extending or flexing the potentially unstable cervical spine.

open.q: Which basic airway-opening manoeuvre must be used instead of head tilt-chin lift when cervical spine injury is suspected?

questions.q: Why is an oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway contraindicated in a semiconscious patient who still has an intact gag reflex?
options: It blocks the vocal cords directly
It can precipitate vomiting, laryngospasm, and aspiration
questions.explain: Stimulating the posterior pharyngeal wall in a patient with a preserved gag reflex induces retching, vomiting, and laryngospasm; a nasopharyngeal airway is better tolerated in obtunded patients with an intact gag reflex.

open.q: Why should an oropharyngeal airway not be inserted in a patient with an intact gag reflex?
accept: It can trigger vomiting, laryngospasm, and aspiration

questions.q: Which haemodynamic pattern characterizes early neurogenic shock following a high thoracic or cervical spinal cord transection?
options: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry extremities
Hypotension with marked tachycardia and cold, clammy skin
Hypertension with bradycardia and bounding pulses
Normal blood pressure with isolated raised JVP
questions.explain: Loss of sympathetic vasomotor and cardioaccelerator tone in high spinal cord injury causes peripheral vasodilation (warm skin, hypotension) and unopposed vagal tone (bradycardia).

open.q: What distinctive heart rate and skin temperature findings distinguish neurogenic shock from hypovolaemic shock?
accept: Low heart rate and warm dry skin

questions.q: A 30-year-old man arrives in the emergency room after massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding with a pulse of 132 bpm, blood pressure of 82/50 mmHg, respiratory rate of 32/min, and confusion, corresponding to >30% blood volume loss. Which ATLS class of haemorrhagic shock does this represent?
options: Class I haemorrhage (<15% blood volume loss)
Class III haemorrhage (30-40% blood volume loss)
Class II haemorrhage (15-30% blood volume loss)
questions.explain: Class III haemorrhagic shock (30-40% blood loss, ~1500-2000 mL) is the threshold where systolic hypotension, marked tachycardia (>120 bpm), tachypnoea (>30/min), and altered mental status manifest.

open.q: At what percentage of acute blood volume loss (ATLS class) does systolic hypotension typically first appear in haemorrhagic shock?

questions.q: Which three bedside clinical criteria constitute the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score for identifying patients with suspected infection at high risk of poor sepsis outcomes?
options: Respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation and systolic BP ≤100 mmHg
questions.explain: The qSOFA bedside screen assigns 1 point each for respiratory rate >= 22/min, altered mental status, and systolic BP <= 100 mmHg; a score >= 2 warrants urgent evaluation for sepsis-related organ dysfunction.

open.q: State the three clinical parameters and cutoff values that comprise the qSOFA score for sepsis screening.
accept: Respiratory rate >= 22/min, systolic BP <= 100 mmHg, and altered mental status

questions.q: What is the first-line vasopressor recommended to restore mean arterial pressure (target >= 65 mmHg) in fluid-refractory septic shock?
questions.explain: Noradrenaline is a potent alpha-1 agonist with modest beta-1 activity that reliably increases systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure with fewer arrhythmias than dopamine.

open.q: Which vasopressor is the first-line agent to maintain a mean arterial pressure >= 65 mmHg in septic shock?

questions.q: Which specific antidote is administered intravenously to rapidly reverse life-threatening respiratory depression caused by opioid overdose?
questions.explain: Naloxone is a competitive mu-opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly restores spontaneous ventilation; because its half-life (30-60 minutes) is shorter than many opioids, patients must be observed for recurrent respiratory depression.

open.q: Name the competitive opioid receptor antagonist used as the emergency antidote for opioid-induced respiratory depression.

questions.q: A 24-year-old farmer is brought to the emergency unit with profuse salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, miosis, and bradycardia after spraying insecticide. Which pair of antidotes is indicated?
questions.explain: Organophosphate poisoning irreversibly inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing a cholinergic crisis (SLUDGE/DUMBBELLS); high-dose atropine blocks muscarinic excess (drying bronchorrhoea) while pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase.

open.q: Which two antidotes are used to treat acute organophosphate insecticide poisoning?

questions.q: Which antidote prevents fulminant hepatic necrosis following acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose by replenishing hepatic glutathione stores?
questions.explain: N-acetylcysteine supplies cysteine to restore hepatic glutathione, detoxifying the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI, and is maximally effective when initiated within 8 hours of ingestion.

open.q: Name the intravenous antidote used to prevent liver failure after acute paracetamol overdose.

questions.q: What is the first-line emergency pharmacological treatment to terminate generalized convulsive status epilepticus?
options: IV lorazepam or diazepam; use buccal/rectal alternatives if needed
questions.explain: Rapid-acting benzodiazepines (IV lorazepam 4 mg or IV diazepam 10 mg) enhance GABA-A inhibition to abort seizures immediately, followed by a second-line anticonvulsant such as levetiracetam, phenytoin, or sodium valproate.

open.q: Which class of drugs is the immediate first-line treatment to abort generalized convulsive status epilepticus?

questions.q: Which clinical sign in a patient with acute asthma indicates life-threatening airway obstruction requiring immediate senior resuscitation and ICU involvement?
options: Silent chest on auscultation with feeble respiratory effort and cyanosis
Loud polyphonic expiratory wheezes throughout both lung fields
Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) of 65% predicted
Ability to speak full sentences between breaths
questions.explain: A silent chest indicates airflow is so severely reduced that insufficient air moves through the narrowed bronchi to generate audible wheezing, heralding imminent respiratory arrest.

open.q: What auscultatory finding in acute severe asthma indicates airflow is too low to generate wheezing and signals imminent respiratory arrest?

questions.q: During the initial resuscitation of an adult presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), what is the single most urgent first intervention?
options: IV sodium bicarbonate before fluid resuscitation
Initial isotonic crystalloid replacement, with reassessment
Subcutaneous long-acting insulin as the first intervention
IV potassium before checking serum potassium
questions.explain: Patients in DKA typically have a 5-8 litre fluid deficit; restoring intravascular volume and renal perfusion with 0.9% saline first lowers blood glucose and counter-regulatory hormones before starting fixed-rate IV insulin.

open.q: What is the immediate first resuscitation priority upon diagnosing diabetic ketoacidosis?
accept: Intravenous fluid resuscitation with 0.9% normal saline

questions.q: A 58-year-old man with acute kidney injury has a serum potassium of 7.1 mmol/L and peaked T waves with widened QRS complexes on ECG. Which drug should be administered intravenously first to stabilize the myocardium?
options: Nebulised salbutamol as the sole immediate measure
IV calcium gluconate to stabilize the myocardium
IV furosemide as the sole immediate measure
questions.explain: Intravenous calcium gluconate directly antagonizes potassium-induced cardiac membrane excitability within 1-3 minutes without lowering serum potassium, preventing ventricular fibrillation while insulin-dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly.

open.q: Which intravenous agent is administered first to protect the myocardium against arrhythmias in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes?

questions.q: In the ABCDE approach to assessing a critically ill patient, what must be done before moving from 'A' (Airway) to 'B' (Breathing)?
options: Obtain a full 12-lead ECG and chest radiograph
Complete a detailed family and social history
Measure hourly urine output via catheterization
Recognize and immediately treat any life-threatening airway obstruction
questions.explain: The ABCDE system follows strict physiological priority: life-threatening problems at each step must be identified and stabilized immediately before progressing to the next step.

open.q: What do the five letters of the ABCDE emergency patient assessment framework stand for?

questions.q: What target range for peripheral arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) is recommended after Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC) to avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxic free-radical injury?
options: 94% to 98% once reliable monitoring is available
questions.explain: Once reliable SpO2 monitoring is established post-ROSC, inspired oxygen is titrated to maintain SpO2 between 94% and 98% because hyperoxaemia exacerbates cerebral reperfusion injury.

open.q: What target SpO2 range is recommended during post-resuscitation care after Return of Spontaneous Circulation?

questions.q: What is the standard emergency treatment for severe symptomatic hypoglycaemia in an unconscious adult with established intravenous access?
questions.explain: Unconscious hypoglycaemic patients cannot swallow safely due to aspiration risk and require immediate IV glucose (10% or 20% dextrose, avoiding hypertonic 50% extravasation tissue necrosis), or IM glucagon 1 mg if IV access is unavailable.

open.q: How is severe hypoglycaemia treated in an unconscious adult when intravenous access is present versus when IV access is unavailable?
accept: IV dextrose (10% or 20%) if IV access is present, or IM glucagon 1 mg if no IV access

questions.q: A 29-year-old man stabbed in the left chest becomes severely hypotensive (BP 70/40 mmHg), tachycardic, and hypoxic with distended neck veins, absent left breath sounds, hyper-resonance on the left, and tracheal shift to the right. What is the immediate life-saving bedside intervention?
options: Immediate endotracheal intubation with high PEEP
Immediate chest decompression followed by definitive chest drainage
questions.explain: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis that must be decompressed immediately without waiting for a chest radiograph, relieving trapped intrapleural air that compresses the vena cava and contralateral lung.

open.q: Why must a suspected tension pneumothorax be treated by immediate chest decompression before obtaining a chest radiograph?
accept: Waiting for an X-ray delays life-saving decompression and risks imminent cardiac arrest
It is a clinical emergency causing obstructive shock and cardiac arrest
Obstructive shock progresses rapidly to cardiac arrest

questions.q: Which triad of clinical signs (Beck's triad) characterizes acute cardiac tamponade?
options: Fever, splinter haemorrhages, and new regurgitant murmur
Tachycardia, tachypnoea, and unilateral calf swelling
Hypotension, distended neck veins (raised JVP), and muffled heart sounds
questions.explain: Beck's triad (hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds) results from pericardial fluid accumulation restricting ventricular filling and reducing stroke volume.

open.q: Name the three clinical findings that form Beck's triad in acute cardiac tamponade.
accept: Hypotension, raised JVP (distended neck veins), and muffled heart sounds
Low blood pressure, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds

questions.q: What is the recommended chest compression rate and depth for high-quality adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation?
options: 100 to 120 compressions per minute at a depth of 5 to 6 cm
60 to 80 compressions per minute at a depth of 2 to 3 cm
140 to 160 compressions per minute at a depth of 8 cm
80 to 100 compressions per minute at a depth of 3 to 4 cm
questions.explain: High-quality adult CPR requires compressing the lower half of the sternum at 100-120/min to a depth of 5-6 cm while allowing full chest recoil and minimizing interruptions.

open.q: State the recommended chest compression rate and compression depth for adult CPR.
accept: 100 to 120 compressions per minute and 5 to 6 cm depth
